title: Astrid and the Verdict
premise: Isandro Sterling, a reclusive insurance investigator with a photographic memory, receives two letters from the same hand: one confessing to a murder, the other promising a fortune for silence. The dead man is Edmund Voss, a shipping magnate whose will names Isandro—someone he never met—as executor. Following Voss's ledger of coded payouts, Isandro uncovers a decades-long scheme in which Voss bought loyalty, alibis, and silence from an entire coastal town, and discovers that the 'found family' Voss assembled was built on a crime they all helped bury. In the end, Isandro must choose between closing the case cleanly and exposing the truth that would destroy the only people who ever made them feel at home—and chooses truth, keeping the family but surrendering the inheritance.
about_author: Paloma Zhou is a former maritime insurance clerk who spent eleven years reading claims files before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about paper trails and the people who leave them.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Hand
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Two letters arrive on the same morning: a confession to killing Edmund Voss, unsigned, and a second letter offering payment for silence. Isandro's memory catalogs every detail—the same ink, the same tremor. When Voss's lawyer calls to confirm Isandro as named executor, the case stops being optional. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into reluctant obligation.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. At Voss's cliffside estate for the reading of the will, Isandro meets the beneficiaries: Voss's housekeeper Marisol, his protégé Dane, and his estranged niece Wren—who all live there like a family. The will names Isandro executor and withholds everything until the ledger is decoded. Emotional beat: Isandro's invisibility cracking under the weight of being seen.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The 'ledger' is a framed embroidery sampler in the study; its stitched dates and initials map to insurance claims Voss once denied. Isandro's photographic recall matches each entry to a fire, a drowning, a collapse—all ruled accidents, all paid out through Voss's company. Emotional beat: cold fascination curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What Marisol Kept
chapters.summary: POV alternating: Isandro interviews Marisol, who reveals she was the first beneficiary—a widow whose claim Voss reversed out of guilt, then kept close. Her confession letter matches the anonymous one's handwriting. She insists she wrote it to protect someone else. Emotional beat: tenderness complicated by suspicion.

chapters.title: Dane's Perfect Alibi
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Dane, Voss's protégé and heir apparent, has an airtight alibi for the night of the death—too perfect, rehearsed down to the weather. Isandro recalls Dane once worked claims adjustment and could read the sampler code. A threatening note appears on Isandro's car. Emotional beat: paranoia taking root.

chapters.title: Wren's Inheritance
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren, who never wanted anything from her uncle, shows Isandro childhood letters proving Voss funded the town's church, school, and clinic through the coded payouts—buying a community's silence after a ferry disaster he caused killed eleven people, including Wren's parents. Emotional beat: grief reframed as complicity.

chapters.title: The Ferry File
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Digging into the original ferry claim, Isandro finds Voss falsified the inspection report; the first 'beneficiary' payments were hush money to survivors' families. The confession letter wasn't about Voss's death—it confessed to helping cover the ferry disaster. Someone is confessing to the wrong crime. Emotional beat: vertigo as the real mystery surfaces.

chapters.title: Silence, Priced
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The second letter's sender makes contact: it's Dane, who learned the truth, confronted Voss, and was offered money for silence the night Voss died of a heart attack mid-argument. Dane took the money and let the town believe murder. The confession letter came from Marisol, shielding Dane. Emotional beat: pity warring with duty.

chapters.title: The Verdict Room
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Climax. Isandro gathers the household and lays out the ledger, the ferry file, and both letters. Dane breaks; Marisol begs for mercy; Wren demands the whole truth be public even if it ruins them all. Isandro must decide whether to file the report that ends the Sterling name's usefulness—or bury it like Voss did. Emotional beat: the cost of power made visible.

chapters.title: Executor
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Resolution. Isandro files the full report, voiding the estate but clearing Dane of murder; the found family scatters yet stays bound by shared truth rather than shared secret. Marisol keeps the house as a memorial to the ferry victims; Wren and Isandro begin rebuilding the claims fund honestly. Final beat: Isandro closes the case by finally letting themselves be known.
